title: The Complete Series — Grand Capstone

pts: Units 1–25 built the single lesson, the single unit, and the classroom and learner context surrounding both.
The capstone at Unit 25 established principled eclecticism as this series' guiding philosophy from its very first quarter.
Nothing in the later tiers replaced this foundation — every subsequent poster built directly on top of it.

v: A recent lesson plan; the Part I checklist (see model language)

items: Choose a lesson you taught in the past fortnight.
Check it against eight foundation questions drawn from Part I (see model language).
Mark each as ‘secure’, ‘developing’ or ‘not yet’.
Choose one ‘developing’ area and revisit the relevant unit.
Rewrite one stage of the lesson using what you revisit.
In a DIET practicum, trainees apply the checklist to a peer’s observed lesson (Unit 68).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Were the aims stated in terms of what learners would be able to do? (Unit 9)
Was new language met in context before it was practised? (Unit 6)
Did learners speak more than I did in at least one stage? (Unit 7)
Was feedback timely and focused? (Unit 8)
Did the lesson reach learners of different levels? (Unit 15)
Was the class safe for mistakes? (Unit 22)
Did home languages have a place? (Unit 24)
Did I check learning, not just coverage? (Unit 21)
Secure on aims and climate. Developing on feedback: I corrected everything at once. I will reread Unit 8 and try delayed correction next week.

blocks.x: Nothing in the later parts replaced these foundations; every later unit built on them.

points.sub: From isolated pieces to real communication
pts: Units 26–50 integrated the skills, systems and assessment Tier I had taught separately, through task, interaction, and extensive input at scale.
The fluency-accuracy-complexity trilogy (Unit 29) emerged as one of this series' most transferable, durable analytical tools.
The capstone at Unit 50 marked the series' halfway point, confirming principled eclecticism applies as much to methodology choice as to any single technique.

v: A recording or transcript of one learner task

items: Record a two-minute learner task from a recent lesson, with permission.
Analyse it for fluency, accuracy and complexity (Unit 29).
Identify which of the three the task design encouraged and which it neglected.
Redesign one element of the task (planning time, repetition, a focus-on-form stage) to shift the balance (Unit 28).
Note how the task integrated skills and systems (Unit 26).
Compare two learners doing the same task, one confident and one hesitant.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Analysis of a Class 9 story-retelling task (fictional, written for this book):

lines: Fluency: few pauses, good speed.
Accuracy: frequent past-tense errors (‘he go’, ‘they was’).
Complexity: short, simple clauses; little linking.
Add five minutes of planning with a story map; ask learners to repeat the story to a new partner; then a short focus on past forms from their own recordings.

blocks.x: The fluency, accuracy and complexity trilogy remains one of the most transferable tools in the book because it applies to any task at any level (Skehan 1998).

body: Purpose: to show one task analysed through three lenses. Content: a learner speaking, with three coloured lenses in front labelled fluency, accuracy and complexity, each revealing a different feature. Style: clean. Board version: three overlapping circles around a speech bubble.

items: Audacity (free, open source) or a phone’s voice recorder for recording the task.

blocks.x: Take notes live during the task on a three-column sheet.

pts: Units 51–75 added discourse and pragmatic precision, full genre and CLIL methodology, and EAP, ESP and materials-writing expertise.
Critical language awareness, testing ethics and World Englishes entered explicitly, alongside action research, mentoring and teacher identity.
The capstone at Unit 75 named reflective expertise — continuous, evidence-responsive practice — as this tier's defining achievement.

items: From Part III, list the areas of depth: pragmatics, genre, CLIL, EAP, ESP, materials writing, action research, mentoring, identity, testing ethics, World Englishes.
Choose the one that matters most for your present role.
Write a portfolio entry: what you now know, what you did with it, and the evidence of effect.
Identify one colleague who could benefit from your depth, and one whose depth could benefit you.

lines: Area: genre-based writing (Unit 54). I introduced the teaching–learning cycle for letters of complaint in Class 10. Learners’ letters became better organized, and more of them used polite, firm tone. Evidence: two sets of scripts, before and after, scored with a four-band rubric (Unit 46).

points.sub: Grounding practice in evidence and honest uncertainty
pts: Units 76–100 examined the SLA theories, research methods, and institutional systems underlying everything the first three tiers had built.
Genuine scholarly debate — Universal Grammar, the Critical Period Hypothesis, bilingualism's real cognitive effects — was presented honestly, without false certainty.
The final stretch confronted native-speakerism, linguistic rights, decolonising ELT, and AI's ethical questions directly and without evasion.

v: A list of everyday teaching decisions

items: Choose one everyday decision, for example ‘Should I correct errors during a fluency task?’ or ‘When should my learners start writing in English?’
List the theories and research from Part IV that bear on it (Units 77, 83, 86–88).
Note where the evidence is strong, where it is contested and where it is thin.
Write the decision you will take, with the reasons and the degree of confidence you have.
Plan how you will check whether the decision works for your learners.
Hold a ‘research café’ in which each table takes one decision and reports back.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A trainee’s decision note (written for this book):

lines: Decision: allow learners to plan in Kannada before speaking in English.

Evidence: sociocultural theory supports talk as a tool for thinking (Unit 83); research on bilingualism and translanguaging supports using the full repertoire (Units 71 and 88); evidence on the ideal amount of L1 use is mixed.
Confidence: moderate. Check: compare English output with and without L1 planning over four lessons.

blocks.x: Part IV presented debates such as Universal Grammar and the Critical Period Hypothesis honestly, without false certainty. This note shows the same honesty in a single classroom decision.

body: Purpose: to show a classroom decision supported by evidence of varying strength. Content: a table labelled ‘decision’ standing on legs of different thickness, labelled ‘strong evidence’, ‘contested’ and ‘my own classroom data’. Style: clear and slightly playful. Board version: a table with three legs of different widths.

items: Google Scholar (free) and ERIC (free) for finding research on a specific question.

blocks.x: The decision note kept in the journal with a reminder to review it.

points.h: Principled Eclecticism, From Start to Finish
points.sub: The one idea that never left
pts: Unit 25 first named it; every capstone since has confirmed it applies at every scale, from a single technique to an entire theoretical worldview.
There is no single best method, no single correct theory, and no substitute for informed, context-sensitive professional judgement.
This series' hundred posters are a toolkit and a map, not a script — exactly as Unit 25 first insisted.

v: The teaching philosophy statement from Unit 25, if written

items: Reread the philosophy statement you wrote in Unit 25, or write a short one now from memory.
Underline the sentences that still hold, and cross out any you no longer believe.
Add one sentence for each part of the book that has changed your thinking.
Reduce the result to no more than 150 words.
Share it with a colleague and ask: ‘Can you see this in my teaching?’
Trainees include the revised statement in their final practicum portfolio.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A revised philosophy (written for this book):

lines: I believe learners learn English by using it for real purposes, with support to notice how it works. I choose methods for reasons that fit my learners, not because they are fashionable. I value my learners’ home languages and their Indian English. I assess what they can do, fairly and openly. I read research with respect and scepticism, and I test ideas in my own classroom. I keep learning because my learners keep changing.

blocks.x: There is no single best method, no single correct theory, and no substitute for informed, context-sensitive judgement. The book is a toolkit and a map, not a script.

body: Purpose: to show principled eclecticism as orientation rather than prescription. Content: a compass rose whose four points are labelled particularity, practicality, possibility and evidence; beside it, a closed script book with a line through it. Style: elegant, restrained. blocks.x: The statement written by hand on the inside cover of the teaching journal.

body: N. S. Prabhu’s article ‘There is no best method—why?’ was published in TESOL Quarterly in 1990 and is still widely read in teacher education. Its central idea, that teachers need a developing sense of plausibility rather than a fixed method, has shaped this book from Unit 25 to Unit 100.

points.sub: The picture this series has built
pts: Expert practice combines foundational skill, genuine skill integration, specialised depth, and honest theoretical grounding — all four tiers, held together.
It includes sustained reflection (Unit 9, Unit 67, Unit 75), genuine care for learners (Units 22–23), and honest engagement with the field's real, unresolved debates.
This is a demanding, lifelong picture of expertise — and also, this series hopes, a genuinely achievable and rewarding one.

items: For each part of the book, rate yourself on a four-point scale for three can-do statements (see model language).
Plot the results as a four-axis profile.
Identify one strength and one priority for the next year.
Discuss your profile with a mentor or colleague (Unit 68), who may add evidence you overlooked.
Revisit the profile at the end of the year.
A mentor and mentee complete profiles for themselves and compare them.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Part I: I can plan a lesson with clear, measurable aims and suitable stages.
Part II: I can design a task that integrates skills and balances fluency and accuracy.
Part III: I can use action research to investigate a question in my own classroom.

blocks.x: Expert practice holds all four together, with sustained reflection (Units 9, 67 and 75) and genuine care for learners (Units 22–23). It is demanding, lifelong and, this book hopes, achievable (Tsui 2003).

Continued reading, action research (Unit 67), and engagement with the wider field (Unit 91) keep any teacher's practice current beyond this series' own content.
The reflective, evidence-seeking habits this series modelled throughout matter more, in the end, than any single poster's specific content.

pts: This hundred-poster series was built as a sequenced, evidence-grounded guide from foundational classroom practice through to the field's genuine theoretical and ethical frontiers.
It draws on decades of scholarship across applied linguistics, SLA research, and language-teaching pedagogy, presented as honestly and usefully as space allowed.
Thank you for following it through to its end — may your own practice keep building on it, questioning it, and taking it further.

blocks.x: A letter to a new teacher (written for this book):

lines: Dear Meena, Learn your learners’ names in the first week, and their languages in the first month. Plan every lesson around what they will be able to do. Welcome mistakes; they show you where learning is happening. Try something new each term, and keep a journal of what happens. When a method or a book, including this one, does not fit your class, adapt it with good reasons. With warm wishes, a colleague.

dek: Unit 100 of 100: the series closes. One hundred posters, four tiers, from a single lesson's foundations to the theoretical and ethical frontiers of the field itself.

aims.x: This final unit closes the book. It looks back over the hundred units and four parts, draws out the ideas that have run through all of them, and looks forward to the professional life that continues after the last page. It does not introduce new techniques. Instead, it asks you to assemble what you have built: a view of your own practice from the single lesson to the theoretical and ethical questions of the field, and a plan for keeping that practice alive.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: summarize the purpose and main contribution of each of the book’s four parts;
explain how principled eclecticism connects the whole book, from a single technique to a theoretical stance;
analyse one of your own lessons through the lenses of all four parts;
describe what language-teaching expertise involves, drawing on research on expert teachers;
assess your own development across the four parts and identify priorities;
design a realistic plan for continuing professional development over the next three years;
revise your teaching philosophy statement in the light of the whole book;
share your learning with colleagues, so that expertise is passed on as well as held.

why: Why this matters. A hundred posters of technique and theory only mean something if they add up to a coherent practice. This final poster draws that whole picture together.

background.x: The book began with a single lesson and a single classroom. Part I (Foundations, Units 1–25) built the essential craft: sounds, vocabulary, grammar in context, classroom management, feedback, lesson and unit planning, assessment, affect and inclusion. Part II (Skill Integration, Units 26–50) joined these pieces into communication through tasks, interaction, extensive input, projects and communicative assessment. Part III (Advanced Pedagogy, Units 51–75) added depth: discourse and pragmatics, genre, CLIL, EAP and ESP, materials writing, action research, mentoring and teacher identity. Part IV (Theory & Research, Units 76–100) examined the theories, research methods, institutions and ethical debates beneath all of these.

One idea has run through all four parts. In 1990, N. S. Prabhu, reflecting on his work in Bangalore, argued that there is no best method, and that what matters is the teacher’s developing sense of plausibility about how learning happens (Prabhu 1990). B. Kumaravadivelu (2006) developed this into a postmethod pedagogy guided by particularity, practicality and possibility. Unit 25 called the resulting stance principled eclecticism: choosing and combining approaches for reasons that fit a particular class. Each later capstone (Units 50 and 75) confirmed that this stance applies at every scale, from choosing an activity to weighing competing theories of acquisition.

Research on teacher expertise supports this picture. Amy Tsui’s (2003) study of ESL teachers in Hong Kong found that expert teachers were distinguished less by knowing more techniques than by integrating their knowledge, responding to their particular contexts, and continually treating their practice as a problem to be explored. Donald Schön (1983) described professional expertise as reflection-in-action, and Simon Borg (2006) showed how teachers’ beliefs shape and are shaped by what they do. Expertise, in this view, is not a destination but a way of working.

In India, NEP 2020 expects every teacher to take part in at least fifty hours of continuing professional development each year and envisages teachers as reflective professionals with autonomy in pedagogy (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020: paras 5.15–5.16) [VERIFY paragraph numbers]. NCF 2023 treats the teacher as central to curriculum renewal (NCERT 2023). DIETs, cluster resource centres, teacher circles and online platforms offer structures for this development. This book has tried to serve those structures: a sequenced guide that teachers, teacher educators and trainees can use, question and take further.

items: Four-part lesson analysis. One of your lessons analysed through the foundations checklist, the fluency–accuracy–complexity lens, an area of depth and a theory-to-decision note.
Expertise profile. A four-axis self-assessment with evidence, a colleague’s view and one priority for the year.
Revised philosophy. A teaching philosophy of no more than 150 words showing how the whole book has shaped your practice.
Professional plan. A three-year development plan with an action research question, reading and community commitments.
Which unit of this book has most changed what you do in the classroom?
Which idea did you resist at first, and how do you see it now?
Where do you now feel expert, and what evidence supports that?
Which debate from Part IV do you think will matter most for Indian classrooms in the next decade?
Who helped you most in becoming the teacher you are, and how can you do the same for someone else?
What question will you still be asking at the end of your career?

perm: All checklists, analyses, plans, philosophy statements, profiles and letters are original and written for this book. Learner recordings used for analysis require consent from learners and parents. Screenshots of Google Forms, Google Sites, Google Sheets, Google Slides, Google Scholar, ERIC, DIKSHA, Zotero, Audacity or Canva require permission or replacement with original illustrations.
next: With thanks. This series was compiled as a sequenced guide for teachers, researchers, and anyone building genuine expertise in English Language Teaching, from the ground up.

terms.def: The ongoing learning teachers undertake throughout their careers, through training, reading, reflection, research and collaboration with colleagues, for example in DIET programmes or teacher networks.
A self-assessment in which a teacher rates their own knowledge and skills across several areas, supported by evidence and a colleague’s view, to set priorities for professional development.

A form of practitioner research in which teachers and learners work together to understand puzzles in their classroom life, using normal teaching activities as the means of investigation (Allwright and Hanks 2009).

Continuing, self-directed learning across one’s life and career, beyond formal education; for teachers, it includes reading, reflection, peer learning and classroom inquiry long after initial training.

An approach to teaching based on the postmethod condition and the parameters of particularity, practicality and possibility, which positions teachers as theorizers of their own practice (Kumaravadivelu 2001).
Combining techniques from different methods on the basis of a coherent rationale suited to the context, rather than mixing them at random.

Thinking about and adjusting one’s practice while it is happening, such as changing an activity mid-lesson when learners are confused (Schön 1983). It contrasts with reflection-on-action, which takes place after the event.

A teacher’s own developing understanding of how learning happens, which guides classroom decisions (Prabhu 1990). Prabhu argued it matters more than any one method, and that it stays alive through reflection and engagement with ideas.

The knowledge, skill and judgement that develop as teachers gain experience and reflect on it, allowing them to read situations quickly and respond flexibly. Experience alone does not guarantee expertise; reflection and learning are essential.
A short written account of a teacher’s beliefs about learning and teaching, with examples from practice. It is often used for reflection, professional portfolios and job applications.
